claims.text: The initially solid Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles form a single-phase solid solution.
Multicomponent chemical complexity increases configurational entropy relative to a single-metal nanoparticle.
Higher configurational entropy elevates the onset temperature of premelting and melting.
Multicomponent chemical complexity alters the latent heat signature of premelting and melting relative to single-metal nanoparticles.
Configurational-entropy contributions to Gibbs free energy persist close to the melting interval in multicomponent alloys.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the solid phase by creating an energetic barrier to atomic rearrangement during premelting.
Multiple element species raise the energy threshold required for atomic mobility and disorder.
Single-metal nanoparticles melt at lower temperatures because their melting is primarily driven by thermal activation.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will have a statistically significantly higher melting onset than single-metal nanoparticles under the same thermal ramp.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will exhibit latent heat values different from those of single-metal nanoparticles under the same thermal ramp.
Cooling rate can materially change the phases and microstructure obtained from a multicomponent melt.
Controlled cooling will consolidate the Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu solid solution.
Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles have well-characterized premelting and melting behavior suitable as baselines under identical conditions.
The proposed effect should apply when HEA and baseline nanoparticles have similar size distributions and low oxidation and defect concentrations.
Nanoparticle surface or support interactions can alter apparent thermal stability and confound attribution to configurational entropy.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that high vacuum eliminates surface effects, whereas the falsification rule treats surface effects as a possible explanation for shifts observed under those conditions. High vacuum may reduce environmental effects but does not eliminate intrinsic nanoparticle surfaces or support interactions.
